explanation.body:
The initial momentum is $p=mu$. The horizontal speed stays constant, so $u=v\cos\theta$ and the horizontal momentum change is zero.

The vertical momentum starts at zero and ends at $mv\sin\theta$ downwards. The change is therefore $m(u/\cos\theta)\sin\theta=mu\tan\theta=p\tan\theta$ downwards.

perOption.A: Uses the initial horizontal momentum as the vertical change.
perOption.B: Doubles the initial momentum as if it reversed direction with unchanged magnitude.
perOption.C: Uses $p$ as the magnitude of the final momentum when resolving vertically.

difficultyReason: The student must resolve the impact momentum and use the unchanged horizontal component.
misconception: Using initial momentum as the impact momentum magnitude
transcription:
A stone is thrown horizontally from the top of a cliff with an initial momentum $p$ and hits the ground at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal. The path of the stone from the cliff to the ground is as shown in the diagram.

[The stone leaves the top of the cliff with a horizontal rightward momentum arrow labelled $p$. Its dashed path curves downwards to the ground, where it makes an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal.]

Ignoring the effects of air resistance, which of the following expressions gives the change in the momentum of the stone from the point of launch to the point it hits the ground?

A $p$
B $2p$
C $p\sin\theta$
D $p\tan\theta$

explanation.body:
Forward friction from the belt accelerates the boxes from rest to $0.80\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. By Newton’s third law the boxes exert an equal backward force on the belt, so an equal forward force maintains its speed.

The required horizontal force is $F=v\,\mathrm{d}m/\mathrm{d}t=(0.80)(2.5)=2.0\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Confuses zero resultant force on the belt with zero applied force.
perOption.B: Halves the momentum gained per second, although every box gains the full belt speed.
perOption.C: Underestimates the momentum transfer from accelerating the full mass flow to belt speed.

difficultyReason: The student must apply the momentum-rate law to a mass flow and identify the force on the belt.
misconception: Constant belt speed implies zero applied force

explanation.body:
The upthrust equals the floating pyramid’s weight and is given by the weight of displaced water. Inverting the pyramid requires a greater submerged depth to displace the same volume, so the pressure difference from the surface to the lowest point increases.

For a floating object, $\rho_w V_wg=\rho_o V_og$, so $V_o/V_w=\rho_w/\rho_o$. The ratio is the same for objects of the same density in water.

perOption.A: This statement is true because the same displaced volume requires different submerged depths in the two orientations.
perOption.B: This statement is true because the pyramid still floats and its weight is unchanged.
perOption.C: Correct. The pressure difference increases when the pyramid floats inverted.
perOption.D: This statement is true because $V_o/V_w=\rho_w/\rho_o$ for a floating object.

difficultyReason: The student must distinguish displaced volume from submerged depth when the pyramid is inverted.
misconception: Equal displaced volume implies equal submerged depth

explanation.body:
The decrease in gravitational potential energy supplies both the increase in kinetic energy and the energy transferred to the surroundings. The energy lost to the surroundings is $mg\Delta h-(\tfrac12mv^2-\tfrac12mu^2)$.

Substituting gives $0.80[9.81(10)-\tfrac12(4.0)^2+\tfrac12(1.2)^2]=72.7\ \mathrm{J}\approx73\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Gives approximately the kinetic energy gain, which stays with the rock.
perOption.B: Roughly halves the gravitational potential energy loss without accounting for the measured kinetic energy gain.
perOption.D: Counts the entire gravitational potential energy decrease as energy transferred to the surroundings.

difficultyReason: The student must calculate both the potential energy loss and the kinetic energy gain.
misconception: Confusing kinetic energy gain with energy dissipated
transcription:
A rock of mass $0.80\ \mathrm{kg}$ is projected horizontally with a speed of $1.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ from the top of a hill. The rock falls through a vertical distance of $10\ \mathrm{m}$ before hitting the ground with a speed of $4.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

What is the energy lost by the rock to the surroundings during its fall?

A $5.7\ \mathrm{J}$
B $39\ \mathrm{J}$
C $73\ \mathrm{J}$
D $79\ \mathrm{J}$

explanation.body:
The car moves at constant velocity, so its kinetic energy stays constant. The motor supplies the rate of increase of gravitational potential energy plus the rate of work against resistance.

Thus $P=mg\Delta h/t+Fd/t=70(9.81)(20\sin30^\circ)+120(20)=9267\ \mathrm{W}\approx9300\ \mathrm{W}$.

perOption.A: Includes only the power used to overcome resistance.
perOption.B: Subtracts the power used to overcome resistance from the rate of gaining gravitational potential energy.
perOption.D: Uses the full along-track speed as the vertical speed when calculating the gravitational contribution.

difficultyReason: The student must combine the rate of climbing with the power used to overcome resistance.
misconception: Subtracting resistive power from the required motor power
transcription:
A toy car of mass $70\ \mathrm{kg}$ is moving at a constant velocity of $20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ up a track that is inclined at an angle of $30^\circ$ to the horizontal.

A constant resistive force of $120\ \mathrm{N}$ acts on the toy car throughout its motion.

What is the power supplied by the motor of the toy car?

A $2400\ \mathrm{W}$
B $4500\ \mathrm{W}$
C $9300\ \mathrm{W}$
D $16000\ \mathrm{W}$

explanation.body:
The linear speed is distance divided by time, or $\omega r=2\pi r/T$. Since $30\ \mathrm{s}$ is half a revolution, the speed is $2\pi(200)/(2\times30)=20.9\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\approx21\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

The average velocity magnitude is displacement divided by time, so it is $2(200)/30=13.3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\approx13\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.B: Uses the arc length to calculate average velocity.
perOption.C: Uses the full circumference for the distance travelled in 30 seconds.
perOption.D: Uses the full circumference for linear speed and the arc length for average velocity.

difficultyReason: The student must distinguish a semicircular path length from the straight-line displacement.
misconception: Using distance travelled to calculate average velocity
transcription:
A car moves from points P to Q along a horizontal semicircular path with constant speed. The radius of the path is $200\ \mathrm{m}$ and the time taken to complete the trip is $30\ \mathrm{s}$.

[A dashed upper semicircle runs from P on the left to Q on the right. The radius from the centre to Q is marked $200\ \mathrm{m}$. Tangent arrows point up at P and down at Q.]

Which row shows the magnitudes of the linear speed and average velocity of the car?

Each row lists linear speed and average velocity in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, respectively.
A 21, 13
B 21, 21
C 42, 13
D 42, 21

explanation.body:
By Newton’s third law the car’s force on the bridge has magnitude equal to the normal force $N$ on the car. At the crests of P and Q, $W-N=mv^2/r$, so P’s smaller radius gives $N_P<N_Q$.

At the bottom of R, $N_R-W=mv^2/r$, while on flat S, $N_S=W$. Hence $N_P<N_Q<N_S<N_R$.

perOption.A: Places the dip below the flat bridge, although upward centripetal acceleration requires the normal force in the dip to exceed the weight.
perOption.C: Reverses P and Q, although P’s tighter crest gives a smaller normal force.
perOption.D: Places the flat bridge below the crests, where downward centripetal acceleration makes the normal force smaller than the weight.

issues: The working continues on page 3. Page 2 says to compare the highest points and claims the normal force is largest there, but the equations compare the crests of P and Q with the bottom of R. The question omits the comparison positions.
difficultyReason: The student must compare both the direction and magnitude of the centripetal force at the bridges’ midpoints.
misconception: Equating the normal force with the centripetal resultant

explanation.body:
Gravity provides the centripetal force, so $GMm/r^2=mv^2/r$. This gives $v^2=GM/r=-\phi$.

For the new orbit, $v_1=v\sqrt{\phi_1/\phi}=v\sqrt{(-16)/(-25)}=\tfrac45v$.

perOption.B: Uses the ratio of potential magnitudes directly as the speed ratio.
perOption.C: Inverts the potential ratio before taking the square root.
perOption.D: Inverts the potential ratio and omits the square root.

difficultyReason: The student must connect circular orbital speed to potential before taking a ratio.
misconception: Orbital speed is proportional to gravitational potential magnitude
transcription:
A satellite orbits around the Earth with a linear speed of $v$. The gravitational potential of that orbit is $-25\ \mathrm{MJ\,kg^{-1}}$. The thrusters of the satellite are then fired and it now moves to a new orbit where the gravitational potential is $-16\ \mathrm{MJ\,kg^{-1}}$.

What is the linear speed of the satellite in the new orbit?

A $\frac45v$
B $\frac{16}{25}v$
C $\frac54v$
D $\frac{25}{16}v$

explanation.body:
The limiting case for reaching Planet Y has kinetic energy approaching zero at the potential maximum Q. From Q to R, conservation of energy gives a kinetic energy gain equal to the decrease in gravitational potential energy.

The limiting impact energy is $E_{\mathrm{k},R}=m(\phi_Q-\phi_R)=5.0[-1.2-(-62.0)]=304\ \mathrm{MJ}$.

perOption.A: Reverses the mass comparison indicated by Y’s much more negative surface potential for planets of similar size.
perOption.B: Treats a potential maximum as a compulsory stopping point, although an object launched above the threshold passes Q with positive speed.
perOption.C: Uses the surface-to-surface potential difference instead of the rise from P to Q.
perOption.D: Correct. This is the limiting impact energy.

issues: The key’s zero kinetic energy at Q represents a threshold. The object must pass Q with positive kinetic energy to reach R, so 304 MJ is the limiting lower bound.
difficultyReason: The student must identify the potential barrier and use the drop from its peak to calculate the limiting impact energy.
misconception: Using the surface-to-surface potential difference as the launch barrier
transcription:
Points P and R are points on the surfaces of Planets X and Y respectively. The graph shows how the gravitational potential $\phi$ along the line PR varies with distance from the centre of Planet X. At point Q the gravitational potential is maximum. Both planets are approximately the same size.

[The horizontal axis is distance, with Planet X at the left and Planet Y at the right. The vertical axis is $\phi$ in $\mathrm{MJ\,kg^{-1}}$. The curve rises from $-10.5$ at P to a maximum of $-1.2$ at Q and falls to $-62.0$ at R.]

An object of mass $5.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ is projected from the surface of Planet X towards Planet Y along the line PQR.

Which statement is correct?

A Planet X is heavier than Planet Y.
B The object comes to rest at point Q.
C The minimum kinetic energy that the object must be projected with for it to reach Planet Y is $258\ \mathrm{MJ}$.
D The minimum kinetic energy that the object has just before it hits the surface of Planet Y is $304\ \mathrm{MJ}$.

explanation.body: Gas molecules exert pressure by transferring momentum to the walls when they collide with them. Compression increases the rate of wall collisions and hence the momentum transferred per unit time per unit wall area, raising the pressure.

perOption.A: At constant temperature the average molecular speed stays constant in the kinetic model.
perOption.B: Reduced intermolecular spacing accompanies compression, while pressure comes directly from momentum transfers to the walls.
perOption.C: Counts collisions between molecules, which transfer momentum within the gas.

difficultyReason: The student must connect pressure to momentum transferred to the walls during collisions.
misconception: Pressure is caused directly by intermolecular collisions

explanation.body:
For the isothermal expansion, $\Delta U_1=Q+W_1=0$, so $-W_1=Q$, where $W_1$ is work done on the gas. For the adiabatic compression, $\Delta U_2=0+W_2=W_2$.

The compression curve lies above the isothermal curve over the same volume range, so its area gives $W_2>|W_1|=Q$. The net internal energy increase is therefore greater than $Q$.

perOption.A: Assumes that returning to the original volume also restores the original temperature.
perOption.B: Underestimates the compression work, whose pressure–volume area exceeds that of the expansion.
perOption.C: Assumes the work done on the gas during compression cancels the work done by the gas during expansion.

difficultyReason: The student must apply the first law twice and compare work magnitudes using the pressure–volume curves.
misconception: Returning to the initial volume restores internal energy

explanation.body: In one period $T$, the particle travels a total distance $4x_0$, where $x_0$ is the amplitude. Its average speed is $4x_0/T=4x_0/(2\pi/\omega)=2\omega x_0/\pi=2v_0/\pi$.

perOption.A: Uses the zero net displacement to calculate average speed.
perOption.B: Averages the minimum and maximum speeds as though the speed varied linearly with time.
perOption.C: Uses one amplitude as the distance covered in a full period.

difficultyReason: The student must identify the total distance per cycle and relate maximum speed and period to angular frequency.
misconception: Using displacement or amplitude as the distance in a full cycle
transcription:
The maximum speed of a particle in simple harmonic motion is $v_0$.

What is the average speed of this particle in one period?

A zero
B $\frac{v_0}{2}$
C $\frac{v_0}{2\pi}$
D $\frac{2v_0}{\pi}$

explanation.body: In steady forced oscillation, the body follows the external periodic force. Its oscillation frequency equals the driving frequency.

perOption.A: Confuses forced oscillation with free oscillation at the natural frequency.
perOption.B: Ignores that the external periodic force fixes the steady oscillation frequency.
perOption.D: Treats the steady response frequency as a compromise between the natural and driving frequencies.

difficultyReason: The student only needs to recall which frequency determines the steady forced response.
misconception: Confusing the natural and driving frequencies

explanation.body: Air molecules just to the left of P have positive displacement, towards P. Those just to the right have negative displacement, also towards P. The molecules are therefore crowded together at P, so P is a point of compression.

perOption.B: Infers motion to the right from a snapshot, although the wave’s direction of travel is unspecified.
perOption.C: Confuses zero displacement with zero speed, although the particle’s kinetic energy is greatest at equilibrium.
perOption.D: Places maximum acceleration at zero displacement, where the restoring acceleration is zero.

issues: The key describes the neighboring particles as moving towards P. The snapshot establishes their displacements towards P, which is sufficient to identify compression.
difficultyReason: The student must infer compression from spatial displacements and distinguish those displacements from velocities.
misconception: Reading particle velocity directly from a displacement snapshot

explanation.body:
Let $I_0$ be the intensity after P and $\theta$ the angle between P and Q. By Malus’ law the intensity after Q is $I_1=I_0\cos^2\theta$.

After R, $I_2=I_1\cos^2(90^\circ-\theta)=I_0\cos^2\theta\sin^2\theta=\tfrac{I_0}{4}\sin^2(2\theta)$. This is zero at both $0^\circ$ and $90^\circ$, so the detector intensity first increases and then decreases.

perOption.A: Assumes that crossed outer sheets block all light at every intermediate orientation of Q.
perOption.B: Tracks the improving alignment of Q with R but overlooks the declining transmission through Q.
perOption.D: Assumes that the detector starts with positive intensity, although Q and R are initially crossed.

difficultyReason: The student must apply Malus’ law twice with complementary angles and interpret the resulting intensity.
misconception: Applying Malus’ law to only one filter
transcription:
Three polaroid sheets P, Q and R are placed along a straight line between a lamp and a detector.

[From left to right the diagram shows the lamp, sheets P, Q and R, and the detector along a dashed line. The polarisation directions of P and Q are parallel and that of R is perpendicular to them.]

Initially, the directions of polarisation of P and Q are parallel but normal to the direction of polarisation of R.

What happens to the intensity $I$ recorded by the detector when Q is rotated slowly through an angle of $90^\circ$ until its direction of polarisation is parallel to that of R?

A $I$ remains unchanged.
B $I$ increases throughout.
C $I$ increases and then decreases.
D $I$ decreases and then increases.
